segments.say: Elena is standing in a row of twenty singers in a small church hall on a cold winter evening. The radiators tick. Folding chairs fill the room, and almost every one of them is taken by somebody's parents, partners, neighbours and friends. It's the community choir's winter concert, and in a few minutes, for the very first time in her life, Elena is going to sing eight bars on her own.

show.cap: A small church hall in winter

segments.say: A quick word about Elena before we go any further. She's imagined. She's someone we've pictured together, to keep us company tonight. She's thirty-eight, she repairs old clocks in a little workshop near the station, and she joined the choir a year ago because a friend dragged her along. Nothing about her stands for a real person, and nothing in her evening is a case study.

The piano plays the opening chords. The conductor gives a small nod. Elena takes one step forward from the row, lifts her chin, and sings. Her voice is a little thin on the first note, and then it settles, and the eight bars go by almost before she knows it. She steps back into the row. The choir comes in behind her. It went fine. Better than fine, really.

And that's when she feels it. A warmth that starts somewhere in her cheeks and spreads outwards, across her face, up to her ears, down her neck, as if someone had opened an oven door right in front of her. She knows exactly what it is. She's blushing. And she knows that every person in those folding chairs can probably see it.

Here's the strange part. Nothing went wrong. She didn't forget the words or crack on a high note. Nobody laughed. If anything, people are smiling at her kindly. And still her face is glowing like a lantern, and the more she thinks about it, the warmer it seems to get. Why would a body do that, at the very moment it's being looked at?

A small hall like this one, warm against the winter outside, with rows of chairs and an old piano. It's an ordinary place. But for a few seconds tonight, it was the place where Elena's face turned red in front of a hundred people.

show.cap: A small hall, a winter concert

segments.say: We'll stay with Elena through the rest of her concert, and the walk home afterwards, and as we go we'll follow one small question all the way down. Why do we blush? It's one of the most familiar things a human face does, and one of the most puzzling. By the end, I hope your own blushes will feel a little less like a betrayal, and a little more like something quite wonderful.

show.title: Tonight, we'll explore
items: Why only humans seem to blush
What actually happens in your skin
A slow walk home to sleep

segments.say: Let me say how we'll do this. Every study we mention tonight is real, published research, and I'll tell you who did it and roughly when. Where scientists aren't sure, I'll say so. Blushing turns out to be one of those topics where the honest answer is often, we're still working on it, and that's part of what makes it interesting.

And this is a calm video. There's no rush. If you're listening in bed, or with your eyes closed, that's exactly right. The first half is a gentle walk through the science, and the second half is a slow, quiet walk home through a winter night, with nothing to learn at all. You can drift off whenever you like. Nothing important will be lost.

So let's go back to the hall. The choir is singing its last song now, something slow and old. Elena is singing too, with the others, safely hidden in the sound. But her cheeks are still warm. She can feel her pulse in them. And a small part of her mind, the part that won't stop asking questions even during a concert, is wondering what on earth is going on in her face.

It's a question people have been asking for a very long time. Long before anyone could measure blood flow or scan a brain, writers and doctors noticed that a red face seemed to give away what a person was feeling inside, whether they liked it or not. A blush can't be faked very easily, and it can't be hidden very easily either. That alone makes it unusual.

Maybe you can remember your own last blush. Perhaps someone praised you in front of other people. Perhaps you said something a little silly and noticed everyone noticing. Perhaps you were simply looked at for a moment longer than you expected. Whatever it was, you probably didn't choose to blush. It just arrived, and then it took its time leaving.

We often treat blushing and embarrassment as the same thing, but they aren't quite. You can feel embarrassed without going red, and, as Elena is discovering, you can go red without feeling that anything embarrassing has happened at all. Praise can do it. A compliment can do it. Even being told that you're blushing can do it, and we'll come back to that one later, because it's a strange little loop.

The last chord fades. There's a pause, and then the applause comes, warm and loud and long. The conductor gestures towards the singers, and then, unexpectedly, towards Elena, and the clapping gets a little louder. And of course, right on cue, her face gets a little warmer. She laughs, because what else can you do, and she bows with everyone else.

So, let's begin. And let's begin with a man who sat down, about a hundred and fifty years ago, and tried to make sense of the blush more carefully than almost anyone before him. He collected letters from all over the world, he watched people closely, and he came to a conclusion about blushing that still gets quoted in nearly every paper on the subject today.
